claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

claimant_dispute_unresolved.description: Whether two responsible claimants cannot agree who should claim Child Benefit.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Hello! I'd be happy to help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit.

To assess your eligibility, I'll need to ask you some questions about your circumstances.

First, do you have any children that you're responsible for?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hello! Yes, I do. I have a son named Alex who's 5 years old and lives with me at home.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. So you have Alex who is 5 years old and lives with you.

To continue assessing your eligibility, could you tell me - do you currently live in the UK?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I live in the UK.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great, thank you. A few more questions to assess your eligibility:

Are you the person primarily responsible for Alex's care? For example, do you provide for his daily needs like food, clothes, and general care?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I'm responsible for Alex's care - I look after him day to day, provide his meals, clothes, all of that.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for confirming that. Just a few more questions to complete the assessment:

Is anyone else currently claiming Child Benefit for Alex?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, that's actually part of the issue. Alex's other parent and I are both responsible for him, but we can't agree on who should claim the Child Benefit.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for explaining that. That's an important detail.

Just to clarify - does Alex live with you full-time, or does he split his time between you and his other parent? For example, does he live with you during the week and with the other parent on weekends, or some other arrangement?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, Alex lives with me full-time. He's at home with me all the time.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying that Alex lives with you full-time.

Just a couple more questions to complete the assessment:

1. Is Alex in hospital, in care, or in any residential accommodation arranged by the local council?

2. Is Alex working 24 hours or more per week, or receiving any benefits in his own name (such as Universal Credit)?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, none of that applies. Alex isn't in hospital or in any kind of care or residential accommodation. And he's only 5, so he's not working or getting any benefits in his own name - he's just a normal little boy at school.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for providing all that information. I now have enough details to assess your eligibility for Child Benefit for Alex.

Based on what you've told me:

- Alex is 5 years old (under 16)
- He lives with you full-time in the UK
- You are responsible for his day-to-day care and provide for his needs
- He's not in hospital, care, or working
- No one is currently claiming Child Benefit for him (though there is a disagreement about who should claim)

According to the Child Benefit rules, you would normally qualify for Child Benefit since you're responsible for a child under 16 and you live in the UK, and the child lives with you.

However, there's an important rule: **only one person can get Child Benefit for a child**. The rules state that if you and someone else are both responsible for the same child, you should agree between yourselves who will claim. If you cannot agree, HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will decide who will get it.

Since Alex lives with you full-time and you provide his day-to-day care, you have a strong case for claiming Child Benefit. However, because there's a disagreement with the other parent about who should claim, HMRC would need to make the final decision if you cannot reach an agreement.

Let me provide my formal assessment:

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**You are ELIGIBLE for Child Benefit for Alex.**

You meet all the requirements because:
- Alex is under 16
- You live in the UK
- Alex lives with you full-time
- You're responsible for his day-to-day care

Regarding the disagreement with Alex's other parent: while only one person can claim Child Benefit for a child, the fact that Alex lives with you full-time strongly supports your claim. If you and the other parent cannot reach an agreement, you can still apply, and HMRC will make the determination about who should receive it.

You should proceed with your Child Benefit application. One important note: if either you or your partner has an individual income over £60,000, you may need to pay the High Income Child Benefit tax charge, though you can still claim the benefit.
